title: Novena for Work and Livelihood
kicker: 9 days of offering our work to God
card: For anyone looking for a job, seeking better work or running a business: 9 days of honest work, trust and generosity.
ogDescription: 9 days of prayer for work and livelihood, through St. Joseph, St. Cajetan and St. Homobonus.
description: A 9-day Catholic novena for job seekers, workers and business owners, through St. Joseph, St. Cajetan and St. Homobonus.

epigraph.text: Entrust your works to the LORD, / and your plans will succeed.

closingVerse.text: May the favor of the Lord our God be ours. / Prosper the work of our hands! / Prosper the work of our hands!

saints.name: St. Joseph
saints.bio: Husband of Mary and foster-father of Jesus. A carpenter of Nazareth, he taught his trade to the One people called “the carpenter’s son.” Honored on May 1 as St. Joseph the Worker.
saints.alt: Painting: St. Joseph holding the Infant Jesus, by Guido Reni

saints.name: St. Cajetan
saints.patron: Patron of the unemployed & job seekers
saints.bio: Priest from Vicenza who co-founded the Theatines in 1524 to renew the clergy. He cared for the sick and the poor, trusted in God’s providence, and died in Naples.
saints.alt: Painting: St. Cajetan in a black cassock, by Andrea Vaccaro
saints.openingRole: friend of all who seek work

saints.name: St. Homobonus
saints.bio: Married cloth merchant of Cremona, known for honest trade and generosity to the poor. Canonized by Pope Innocent III in 1199, just over a year after his death.
saints.alt: Painting: St. Homobonus in a merchant’s hood and cap, holding a purse

openingPrayer: Heavenly Father, You made us in Your image and gave us work to do in Your world. You know the needs we bring today: the search for a job, the hope of better and fairer work, the cares of a business and of everyone who depends on it. We trust in Your providence more than in our own anxious efforts. Today we ask St. Joseph, carpenter of Nazareth; St. Cajetan, friend of all who seek work; and St. Homobonus, honest merchant of Cremona, to join their prayers with ours before Your throne, through Christ our Lord.
closingPrayer: Lord Jesus, who worked with Your hands at Nazareth, bless our work and our search for work. Make us honest, diligent and generous, provide what we and those in our care need, and let Your holy will be done.

tips.p: One person leads each part; all respond pray for us and Amen, and say the closing prayers together. The prayers say “we”; if you pray alone, say “I”.

If you can, go to Confession and attend Mass during these 9 days, and keep Sunday as a day of rest. Pair prayer with one prudent step (Day 3): update your CV, ask someone you trust for advice, or talk honestly with your staff. Beware of false shortcuts: illegal recruiters, placement-fee scams and “get rich quick” schemes.

intentionPlaceholder: Write the job search, work or business you are praying for.

days.title: All Who Labor
days.verse: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart; and you will find rest for yourselves. For my yoke is easy, and my burden light.”
days.refl: Jesus calls “all you who labor and are burdened,” and that includes every kind of weariness about work. Some of us are looking for a job and hearing nothing back. Some are stuck in work that is unfair, unsafe or wrong for us. Some carry a business, with wages to pay and customers to keep, and lie awake over it. Jesus does not ask us to pretend things are fine. He asks us to come to Him just as we are, and He promises rest.
days.more: Losing work, or fearing to lose it, touches more than our income. It can shake our sense of who we are and what we are worth. But our dignity does not come from a job title, a salary or a sales report; it comes from being made in God’s image and loved by Him. St. Joseph knew the plain, hardworking life of a village craftsman. We can tell him, and Jesus, exactly where we are.
days.prayer: Heavenly Father, You see the work we have, the work we lack and the work we long for. You know the worry that follows us home and the questions that keep us awake. We come to Jesus as we are, tired and unsure. Through the prayers of St. Joseph, St. Cajetan and St. Homobonus, give us rest in Your presence, the courage to face our situation honestly, and the trust that You have not forgotten us.
days.step: Write a few honest lines about your work situation (what you have, what you need, what you fear) and offer them to God.

days.title: Trust, Not Restless Toil
days.verse: It is vain for you to rise early / and put off your rest at night, / To eat bread earned by hard toil— / all this God gives to his beloved in sleep.
days.refl: The psalm does not praise laziness. It warns against work that trusts only in itself: rising early, putting off our rest at night, eating “bread earned by hard toil,” as if everything depended on us. St. Cajetan is remembered as a saint of Providence. His Theatine priests owned nothing and did not even beg, trusting God to provide. We still work hard, and we still plan. But we can lay our heads down at night, because God gives to His beloved even in sleep.
days.more: The Church asks us to keep Sunday for worship and to set aside work that keeps us from it, remembering that we are more than what we produce (CCC 2184–2185). For the overworked, that can feel impossible; for those without work, Sunday can feel empty. Yet the Lord’s Day is a gift to both: a reminder that our worth is not measured by output, and that the Father holds what we cannot.
days.prayer: Lord God, You give to those You love even in their sleep. Free us from the restless toil that trusts only in our own effort, and from the fear that keeps us working long past what is wise. Through the prayers of St. Cajetan, who trusted in Your providence, and of Our Mother of Perpetual Help, teach us to work hard and rest well, to keep Your day holy, and to leave tomorrow in Your hands.
days.step: This Sunday, go to Mass and set aside some time for real rest, without job listings, work emails or business accounts.

days.title: Ask, Seek, Knock
days.verse: Ask and it will be given to you; seek and you will find; knock and the door will be opened to you. For everyone who asks, receives; and the one who seeks, finds; and to the one who knocks, the door will be opened.
days.refl: Jesus tells us to ask, to seek and to knock, and to keep on doing it. He does not promise that the first door will open, or that every door will. He promises that the Father hears us and gives what is good. Looking for work can mean many silent applications and interviews that lead nowhere. Each one can be offered as a prayer. St. Cajetan, invoked by so many people looking for work, reminds us that we never knock alone.
days.more: Every August 7, crowds line up at the shrine of San Cayetano in Buenos Aires to ask for bread and work. Their faith is simple and persevering. Searching for work is itself work, and it can be tiring and humbling. It helps to treat it like a job: a set time each day, honest follow-up, and a short prayer before each application, interview or sales call. Rejection is not the last word on our worth.
days.prayer: Father, Your Son told us to ask, to seek and to knock. We ask You for honest, fairly paid work, for customers and good opportunities, and for the right people to cross our path. When we hear nothing back, keep us from discouragement and bitterness. Through the prayers of St. Cajetan, friend of all who look for work, and of St. Joseph, help us keep knocking with patience, humility and hope.
days.step: Take one concrete step today: update your CV, send one application, or ask someone you trust about openings or new customers.

days.title: Work Made Holy
days.verse: The LORD God then took the man and settled him in the garden of Eden, to cultivate and care for it.
days.refl: Before there was any sin, God gave the first man work to do: to cultivate the garden and care for it. Work is not a punishment. It is a share in God’s own care for the world. Centuries later, the Son of God spent most of His years on earth in Nazareth, known to His neighbors as “the carpenter’s son.” He learned His trade from St. Joseph. Ordinary work, done well and offered to God, became holy there.
days.more: The Church teaches that work honors the Creator’s gifts and the talents we have received, and can become a path to holiness when united to Christ (CCC 2427). Work is for the person, not the person for work (CCC 2428). In 1955 Pope Pius XII instituted the feast of St. Joseph the Worker on May 1. Whatever our work, at a desk, a counter or a building site, we can offer it to God.
days.prayer: Lord God, You gave us work as a share in Your care for the world, and Your Son worked with His hands at Nazareth. Through the prayers of St. Joseph, the carpenter, help us see the dignity of every honest job, our own and other people’s. Make us diligent and careful in what we do, faithful in small tasks, and glad to offer our work to You, whether anyone notices it or not.
days.step: Do one ordinary task today with extra care, and offer it to God for someone who is looking for work.

days.title: Work That Fits Our Gifts
days.verse: As each one has received a gift, use it to serve one another as good stewards of God’s varied grace.
days.refl: St. Peter reminds us that each of us has received a gift, given to serve one another “as good stewards of God’s varied grace.” The farmer, the nurse, the driver and the shopkeeper each have their own. Work is one of the places where our gifts grow and serve others. Some of us are in jobs that waste our gifts, pay unfairly or wear us down. It is right to ask God for better work, and to seek it wisely.
days.more: The Church teaches that a just wage is the legitimate fruit of work, and that refusing or withholding it can be a grave injustice (CCC 2434). Wanting fair pay, safe conditions and an employer who treats people with respect is not ingratitude. Still, a change of work needs discernment: talking it over with people we trust, weighing what it will cost those who depend on us, and asking where our gifts are truly needed.
days.prayer: Father, You have given each of us gifts to use for others. Lead us to work that fits those gifts, pays fairly, keeps us safe and treats us with respect. Where we must stay for now, give us patience, and courage to speak up for what is right. Through the prayers of St. Joseph, who taught Your Son His trade, of Our Mother of Perpetual Help and of St. Cajetan, guide our choices and open the way You know is best.
days.step: List three gifts or skills that others have thanked you for, and ask God how they might serve in your work.

days.title: Honest Dealings
days.verse: False scales are an abomination to the LORD, / but an honest weight, his delight.
days.refl: In the markets of ancient Israel, a dishonest trader could cheat with a scale that tipped his way. God calls such false scales an abomination, and calls an honest weight His delight. St. Homobonus, a cloth merchant of Cremona, was known for his scrupulous honesty in trade. Whether we run a small store, sell online or manage a company, God cares how we price, measure, advertise and pay. Honest business is a way of loving our neighbor.
days.more: Honesty runs both ways. Owners owe their workers just wages, paid on time, and their customers fair prices and the truth about what they sell. Workers owe their employers an honest day’s work. The Church names business fraud and unjust wages as sins against the seventh commandment (CCC 2409). When Pope Innocent III canonized St. Homobonus in 1199, he called him “father of the poor”: his trade served others, not only himself.
days.prayer: God of truth, make us honest in all our dealings. Keep us from cheating, cutting corners, hiding faults or taking advantage of anyone. If we employ others, help us pay fair wages on time and treat our workers with respect. If we serve customers, help us deal with them truthfully. Through the prayers of St. Homobonus, the honest merchant, make our work a sign of integrity, even when honesty costs us.
days.step: Look at one part of your work or business (a price, a report, a wage, a promise) and make sure it is completely honest.

days.title: Wisdom in Decisions
days.verse: But if any of you lacks wisdom, he should ask God who gives to all generously and ungrudgingly, and he will be given it.
days.refl: Work brings hard decisions: which offer to accept, whether to leave a job, whether to hire, expand, cut back or close. St. James tells us simply to ask God for wisdom, and assures us that He gives it generously and ungrudgingly. St. Joseph faced decisions he could never have planned for. He listened to God, then acted without delay. We can bring every decision to prayer, gather the facts, seek good counsel, and then choose in peace.
days.more: God guided St. Joseph in dreams; for most of us, discernment comes more quietly. It grows as we pray honestly, talk with people who know us and know the work, think of everyone the choice will affect, and notice where we find lasting peace. St. Homobonus was a married man running a business, not a monk. His holiness grew in ordinary decisions: what to sell, what to charge, how much to give away.
days.prayer: Lord, You give wisdom generously to all who ask. Give us clear minds and honest hearts in every decision about our work: offers to weigh, people to hire, risks to take or avoid. Keep us from acting out of panic, pride or greed. Through the prayers of St. Joseph, who listened and obeyed, and of St. Homobonus, who did business with a clean conscience, help us choose what is right and leave the results to You.
days.step: Bring one work decision to prayer today, then talk it over with someone wise and honest before you decide.

days.title: Honest Work, Open Hands
days.verse: The thief must no longer steal, but rather labor, doing honest work with his [own] hands, so that he may have something to share with one in need.
days.refl: St. Paul gives work two purposes: to earn honestly, and to have something to share. Work is never only for ourselves. It provides for our own, and it lets us open our hands to people in need. St. Homobonus did well in business, yet he and his wife lived simply, and he gave much of his money to the poor. Generosity keeps our work from turning into greed, and keeps our hearts free for God.
days.more: St. Cajetan cared for the poor and the sick in practical ways. In his home city of Vicenza he founded a hospital for the incurably ill, and he served the sick himself. Generosity can be wise as well as warm. Even when money is tight, there is something we can give: a fair chance to someone looking for work, honest advice to a struggling neighbor, a little set aside for the poor.
days.prayer: Generous Father, everything we have comes from You. Bless our work so that we may provide for those in our care and have something to share with those in need. Keep us from greed, envy and the love of money, and open our hands to the poor. Through the prayers of St. Homobonus, father of the poor, and of St. Cajetan, who served the sick and the poor, make us generous in good times and in lean ones.
days.step: Share something from your work this week with someone in need: a donation, a meal, a job lead, or your skill given freely.

days.title: Gratitude & Trust in God’s Will
days.verse: And whatever you do, in word or in deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him.
days.refl: St. Paul asks us to do everything in the name of Jesus, giving thanks. We end these nine days not by demanding an outcome, but by giving thanks, because God has heard every prayer and answers in the way that is truly best. Some of us may have found work; some are still waiting; some face a business that may not survive. With St. Joseph, St. Cajetan and St. Homobonus, we place our work and our future in the hands of a faithful Father.
days.more: A closed door, a long search or a business that fails is never a sign that God has abandoned us or that our faith was too weak. The Cross looked like failure too. Looking back over these nine days, we may notice small graces: a kind word, a helpful contact, a clearer mind, a little more peace. Trusting God’s will means we keep praying and working, in peace.
days.prayer: Lord, on this ninth day we thank You for Your faithfulness and for every grace, seen and unseen, that You have given us. Thank you, Our Mother of Perpetual Help, St. Joseph, St. Cajetan and St. Homobonus, for carrying our prayers before Jesus. We entrust our work, our search, our business and all who depend on us to Your loving will, trusting that You will give what is truly good for us.
days.step: Write down three graces you noticed during these nine days, and thank God for them together.

printClosing: May the favor of the Lord our God be ours.
Prosper the work of our hands! Prosper the work of our hands!
